chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-Hasan ibn Ali from his brother al-Husayn ibn Ali ibn Yaqteen from his father Ali ibn Yaqteen from Abu al-Husayn ibn Ali ibn Yaqteen from his father Ali ibn Yaqteen from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) who said:

Indeed, Allah the Exalted did not forbid wine by its name, but He forbade it by its consequence; therefore, whatever has the consequence of wine is wine. He (peace be upon him) commanded and forbade me, saying: 'O Abu Muhammad, do you not hear these questions? No, so do not taste a drop of it, for you will only regret it when it reaches your throat here,' and he pointed with his hand to his throat, saying it three times: 'Did you understand?' She said: 'Yes.' Then Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Whatever is swallowed is impure, a handful of water.' He said it three times.

From him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Umar ibn Udhaynah, who said: I wrote to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) asking him about a man for whom medicine for hemorrhoids is prescribed, and he drinks it with the amount of a sugar cube of solid nabidh (fermented drink), not desiring pleasure by it, but only desiring medicine by it. He said: 'Yes, and even a gulp.' And he said: 'Indeed, Allah the Mighty and Majestic did not make in anything of what He forbade a medicine or a cure.'
ai.seo_question: Is wine prohibited by name or by effect, and does medicine made from it remain forbidden?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) establishes the principle of 'idtirar' (intoxication) as the core cause of prohibition, extending the ruling to any substance with similar effects regardless of its name. It further clarifies that even small amounts of solid fermented drinks used for medicine are impure and not exempt, as Allah did not make a cure within the forbidden substances themselves. This ruling is significant in Shia jurisprudence for determining the purity and consumption of various fermented products.
